utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, Wednesday, the 10th of March, 2010, I would like to greet General Petkovic, first of all, our witness, the accused who are present, the Defence teams, Mr. Scott, and everyone else assisting us. I will now read out two oral decisions. The decision, oral decision on granting time for the hearing of the Witness Zvonko Vidovic. Zvonko Vidovic shall be called as a viva voce witness from the 29th of March to the 1st of April, 2010. The Coric Defence would like to have three hours for its examination-in-chief of this witness. On the 1st of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence asked the Chamber for a total of one hour, or 42 additional minutes, to cross-examine the witness. In addition, the Chamber notes that in a memo dated the 10th of February, 2010, the Stojic Defence asked the Chamber for 48 minutes, or an additional 30 minutes, to cross-examine the witness. In addition, it requested that this additional time be charged to the total time granted to it by the Chamber. On the 5th of February, 2010, the Coric Defence filed a response to the Petkovic motion. On the 9th of February, 2010, the Chamber authorised the Petkovic Defence to file a response to the Coric Defence's response, which was done on the 12th of February, 2010. First of all, with regard to the Petkovic Defence request, the Chamber is of the opinion that one hour for the cross-examination of Zvonko Vidovic is disproportionate with regard to the events that are contained in the 65 ter summary of the testimony that the witness is to be giving. The Chamber believes that an additional 30 minutes should suffice to allow the Petkovic Defence to protect its client's interests. Secondly, as far as the Stojic Defence memo is concerned, the Chamber is of the opinion that in light of the 65 ter summary of the witness's future testimony, and the subjects that the Stojic Defence wants to address with the witness, 30 minutes -- 30 additional minutes should suffice for the Stojic Defence to conduct its cross-examination. The Chamber notes that this additional time of 30 minutes shall be charged to the total time granted to it by the Chamber. As a result, the Chamber hereby decides to allocate the time as follows: The Coric Defence shall have three hours for its examination-in-chief and for any re-examination it might have. And I insist on the word "and." The Prosecution shall have three hours to conduct its cross-examination. The Stojic and Petkovic Defence teams shall have 48 minutes each. Given that no particular requests have been made, the Prlic, Praljak, and Pusic Defence teams shall have 18 minutes each. Second oral decision concerning the Stojic Defence's request for time to conduct an additional cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic and with regard to the Petkovic Defence for additional time for its additional examination, for its re-examination. At a hearing on the 9th of March, 2010, the Stojic Defence asked the Chamber to grant it 30 minutes to conduct an additional cross-examination of Milivoj Petkovic on the grounds that the Prosecution had, in the course of its cross-examination, raised new subjects that concern, in particular, the management of detention centres and the responsibility of Bruno Stojic for such centres. In addition, it requests that this additional time be charged to the total amount of time granted to it by the Chamber. The Petkovic Defence has stated that it is not opposed to the Stojic Defence request. In addition, in the course of the very same hearing, the Petkovic Defence informed the Chamber that it thought it needed about five hours to conduct additional examination of Mr. Petkovic. The Chamber is of the opinion that the Stojic Defence request is founded, in terms of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008, and that it is reasonable to demand additional cross-examination. As a result, the Chamber hereby decides to grant it 30 additional minutes. The Chamber notes the request of the Stojic Defence to have the additional 30 minutes charged to its total time. With regard to the Petkovic Defence request, and in the light of the new subjects -- with regard to the new subjects raised by the Prosecution in the course of its cross-examination, the Chamber hereby decides that the Petkovic Defence shall have two additional hours, in addition to the fifteen additional minutes already granted by the Chamber, for the re-examination of Milivoj Petkovic. The Petkovic Defence shall, therefore, have a total of two hours and fifteen minutes for its re-examination. The Chamber notes that the two additional hours granted to the Petkovic Defence shall be charged to the total amount of time it disposes of. Those are our two oral decisions, handed down unanimously by the Judges present here as well as by the Judge who is absent today, and this was done having examined all the relevant elements and having taken note of all the comments made by the parties. Mr. Scott, I know that you have another 20 minutes. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Without any great hope in the success of my request, and perhaps with the Appeals Chamber -- for the benefit of the Appeals Chamber perhaps tomorrow, or anybody studying this, I would like to request more time for the Petkovic Defence in view of the new topics raised during its cross-examination lasting nine hours and forty minutes, and a series of new topics which some of the Defence teams raised during their cross-examination. And up until now, the total duration is six hours, which means a total duration of fifteen-odd hours. I'd like to remind you that the Defence of General Petkovic had at its disposal only four hours and forty minutes for its examination-in-chief. Now, in view of this decision on the distribution of time, it's not in conformity with the express provisions and guide-lines in these proceedings. And without questioning the right of the Trial Chamber to decide on the time allocated, in view of the circumstances, and to deviate from what was established in the guide-lines, I would like to ask you for a written explanation and an expounding of the ruling, why -- telling us why the Petkovic Defence is this time being given less time than provided for in the guide-lines. And if, in those statements of reason, there is anything except what we have heard in the cross-examination as not being relevant and that we don't need to bring it up again in redirect, the Petkovic Defence is now making a request for leave to appeal your ruling on the allocation of time. So, once again, I'd like to ask you to reassess how much time the Petkovic Defence would actually need, in view of the relevancy of the new topics brought up in the cross-examinations. And we sent you an e-mail last night for a request for three and a half hours, which would be the minimum of the minimum time required. And if you refuse, then I would like to seek leave for certification to appeal the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Since things are being said about appeal, and making the record, and to help assist, that the record be as balanced as possible, let me make just a few brief observations, please. And, first of all, good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Judge Trechsel, and good morning to all those around us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. That is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to Judge Mindua as well. Apologies. Your Honours, I think -- I have no quarrel with the Court's ruling, either in terms of the time that is given to the Stojic Defence or to the ruling on the Petkovic Defence, so I'm not -- I don't rise to my feet to quarrel with the Chamber's ruling, but just to touch on the record. Your Honour, I think it's fair to say, and it would be our position, the Prosecution's position, that no new issues were substantially raised by the Prosecution's cross-examination of Mr. Petkovic. I believe that everything that the Prosecution raised and touched on can fairly be connected to something either raised by the direct examination of Mr. Petkovic, or the co-accuseds' examinations, or the Court's examinations. I'll use the one example in connection with the camps that prompts -- apparently prompts the Stojic Defence to ask for more time, which, again, I don't quarrel with. The Chamber might recall the discussions that were had some weeks ago about redirect -- the scope of redirect and what topics had been raised in direct examination. It was at that time that the Prosecution noted that Ms. Alaburic, in her examination of Mr. Petkovic, had briefly -- ever so briefly raised the question of camps, and it was basically to the effect of two or three questions to the effect of, Well, who was responsible, essentially, for the camps, or what was said, or what the conversation with Mr. Boban about the camps? And the Chamber will recall, hopefully, from just yesterday, it was exactly that very short, but nonetheless presentation on the topic, that I then came back to Mr. Petkovic and said, Well, you've said that you've talked to Boban, and other than disarming and arresting the men, their housing and care was somebody else's responsibility. And then I asked, Well, whose was it? That was a question that was left hanging, if you will, from the direct exam and, I think, begged to be asked by someone. We did that. So just so the record is fair, and in case anyone -- if the Appeals Chamber or anyone looks at this, I just want the record to be -- at least from our perspective, to be added and balanced that the Prosecution does not believe its injected any substantially new topic into the case, other than those which had been already addressed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one sentence. What Mr. Scott has just said is exactly opposed to his request for additional time to examine General Petkovic. I'd like to remind you that my colleague Mr. Scott, in his request, enumerated 18 topics for which he claimed were not raised in the examination-in-chief and that that was the reason for which he was requesting additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has deliberated, has conferred, and we stand by our decision. I, personally, however, would like to point out the following for the benefit of the Petkovic Defence. I, personally, don't believe that any new subjects have been addressed. From the outset, I was of the opinion that the Petkovic -- that when the accused was testifying, it was obvious that the Prosecution would ask questions about the entire indictment. This was to be anticipated. In addition, the guide-lines are quite clear. The Chamber's guide-lines were adopted after an immense amount of work had been done, so that we should have very useful and clear guide-lines for everyone, and these guide-lines clearly state that a Defence team has to tell us, in advance, how much time it requires for its examination-in-chief and, I add, for re-examination. So when a Defence team tells us, I need six hours, in our opinion that means that the Defence has taken all the elements into account, that the six hours includes cross-examination and re-examination. It should be pointed out that the Defence must always have a certain amount of time left for cross-examination, but this should be anticipated in advance. So when we are told, We need six hours, all the elements -- all the factors have been taken into account, including the fact that the Prosecution, in its cross-examination, will address all subjects contained in the indictment; these aren't new subjects. Unfortunately, one has to point out that we are systematically being asked for additional time, and this goes against the spirit and the letter of the guide-lines. Having said that, it is true that five hours amounts to 300 minutes, and two hours and fifteen minutes is not equal to 300 minutes, but let's not confuse quantity and quality. In two hours and fifteen minutes, it's quite possible to address important issues that require additional questions. Additional questions -- additional examination must be directly related to questions put in the cross-examination. So that is the point of additional examination. So I totally accept the Chamber's position. We stand by our decision, and the Chamber doesn't take decisions at random. Everything has been put into the balance, carefully considered. When a decision is handed down, it is done so after having examined all the relevant factors. The Judges aren't a puppet who can just change his opinions. We took a decision. Yesterday, we had the courtesy of informing you of the fact yesterday so that you would know, in advance, what the contents of the decision were. We did that. We proceeded in this manner to facilitate the task for you. So you will have hours and fifteen minutes, and much can be done in that time. Mr. Scott, you have another 20 minutes, and you should conclude within those 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I expect to be able to do so, barring any particular interventions or issues that might arise, but I think we can. First of all, good morning, Mr. Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Scott. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's a technical issue, I'm afraid. It's difficult for the Defence really to operate without the full technical assistance that we're used to. And I see from Judge Trechsel that the Bench is unfortunately in the same boat as the parties. We don't have LiveNote. It's almost half past 9.00, and since the beginning of proceedings we have not had LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar has told me that this is a general problem that the Tribunal is facing. Mr. Scott, we have the transcript, and everything you say will be recorded in the transcript. That is what is essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And as I was saying, Mr. Petkovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed briefly yesterday this concept, if you will, that I put to you or explained to you, in terms of we seem to often have this phenomenon, if I can call it that, in these cases: So when crimes are committed by the so-called other side, the victim side tends to suggest and claim -- and all sides, and I'm not picking on the Croats -- the Serbs, the Muslims, do the same thing. When they are on the victim side, they point to the other side and say, These crimes against us were systematic, they were the result of a master plan, they were co-ordinated from the top, et cetera. And then when one is confronted with the crimes committed -- or allegedly committed by its own side, if you will, then those crimes are frequently referred to or characterised as, Well, these are the random acts of individual bad actors, and, you know, people do get out of control, et cetera, et cetera. You remember that discussion, briefly, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember it being exactly like that. The HVO didn't hide anything. And if there was anything out of control, it would be said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about some of the crimes, some of the more major crimes. Apologies if I cut across. I didn't see the -- all right. Let's talk about some of the crimes, sir, that feature prominently in the -- or alleged crimes, of course, that feature in the indictment. The mass arrest and detention of Muslims in July and thereafter, which you've now, I think, made clear was done on your order, in turn on Mr. Boban's direction, the conduct and operation of the camps, the conditions and treatment in the camps, and I mention one aspect, the starvation of the Muslims at Dretelj, the forced labour which you specifically were on notice of and approved, which we discussed yesterday, large-scale expulsions, Mostar, Stolac, I remind you and the courtroom of the report by Markovic to President Tudjman in the fall of 1993: "Not a single Muslim left in Stolac." I put it to you, sir, that could not have been simply an accident; the continuous shelling of East Mostar; the destruction of mosques and Muslim religious and cultural sites, the crimes at Ahmici, which we talked about yesterday, the atrocities at Stupni Do, the destruction of the Old Bridge at Stari Most; sir, I raise there for this purpose, and I put to you that none of those crimes can be reasonably characterised as the random acts of individual bad actors, can they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we should have to look at each individual case, and we would see that cases like that exist too. But as for Markovic, I don't know who sent him, because he wasn't from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the conducts of the camps to pick and just to pause on one subject, and again our time will be limited, but no one can suggest that the camps which are established and operated clearly on a systematic basis, you can't say the camps are operated based on the random acts of individuals. There was a system in place, there were administrations, there was reporting, there was the need for resources, there were the need for logistics, there was a systematic process for the taking out of prisoners for forced labour. You can't possibly suggest, sir, I put to you, that that is the product -- that those are the products of individual bad acts, can you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that it was the act of individuals, but what I'm saying is that it wasn't everywhere the way you want to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the reality is, sir -- and we don't have time, really, today to beat around the bush, so to speak. The reality is the HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities did nothing to prosecute or punish any of the crimes that I have just put to you, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the HVO and the authorities did prosecute quite a number of people, and there were criminal reports. And this has been proved during this trial for certain acts committed. So you can't say that the HVO did not prosecute its own people or, rather, file criminal reports. Now, I don't want to go into court procedure and how that is done further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a moment. But if I were to represent to you that, for example, based on a conversation with Mr. Siljeg, in which he was asked, Did you, during the time you were the operative zone commander from approximately October 1992 to December 1993, did you ever request or initiate any investigation into alleged war crimes by an HVO officer and soldier, and Mr. Siljeg answered that question, No, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, General. I'm going to object. Where is this from? Is this in evidence? Siljeg didn't come and testify. Do we have an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Siljeg? Will the Trial Chamber be bringing him? Is the Prosecution intending on bringing him at some point? So I think the question is unfair. And if he wishes to confront the gentleman with what Mr. Siljeg said, then I suggest that he confront him with a document and that that be shared with the rest of us to see whether or not I have any further objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, when speaking about Mr. Siljeg, you must refer to a precise document. You certainly have the document's number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only refer at the moment to a consolidated transcript of his interview, which is -- which I can provide in more detail. But it would be at the video page 48 -- video 4806, page 2. But in the interests of time, Your Honour, I won't persist in the question. But I do have a basis and did have a basis for putting the question, and I don't think it has to be in evidence, Your Honour. That has not been the practice in this case, that everything put to a witness in cross-examination has to be in evidence. I have a very firm and good basis for putting the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a statement obviously taken of the gentleman. Now, the Prosecution, in the past, has moved to get statements in even though those individuals were never intended to be called as witnesses. Now we have a statement being introduced that has not been introduced into evidence and the gentleman is not coming. Now the question has been withdrawn. I appreciate that. I also wish to note, for the record, that none of the comments made by the Prosecution, as far as what Mr. Siljeg said, should be evidence and can be considered as evidence at any point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank my colleague Karnavas, and I fully support everything he said. If I may just add, if I remember well the interview which a representative of the Prosecution of this Tribunal had with Mr. Siljeg, and I think Mr. Scott is referring to that interview, which is not in evidence in this case, it is not on the 65 ter list, it was never in the form of a document that would be tendered into evidence in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- I have only limited time. I'm not going to persist in it, although I don't agree with the objections that have been made at all. But we don't have time to debate -- I choose not to debate it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir, I put to you that you said that matters -- that some things were prosecuted, and we'll come to that in a moment. But I put it to you, sir, that, in fact, in fact, nothing -- nothing effective was done to punish or prosecute any of the crimes of the sort that I have mentioned to you this morning, and that's the operation of the camps, the destruction of the Stari Most, the mass expulsions of Muslims from multiple places. Yes, I agree with you, if we go through the documents we will find a case here and there, a random case, but not for places against -- for crimes against Muslims; hardly ever, sir. And that was the case, wasn't it? They just weren't a priority. It wasn't something that the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna authorities were very interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this is quite correct, Mr. Scott, but I seem to recall a case where a young woman was shot when the family was asked to move away, and the author of that crime was, in fact, prosecuted and committed, I think, to an institution. So I think we should not overstate -- you should not overstate the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that's what I attempted to address. I said, I'm sure there were some individual cases. And if that wasn't clear, then I do make that clear. I'm not saying there were not any cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do think that there were a few -- a very few cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the case, though, isn't it, sir? It just simply wasn't a priority for you, it wasn't a priority for the other accused in this case, it wasn't a priority for the Herceg-Bosna authorities. Prosecuting HVO officers and soldiers for crimes against Muslims was just not something that was considered very important or that was pursued only in the most -- except only in the most exceptional cases; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not, you're not right. I'll tell you that from the area of Prozor, more than 20 people were prosecuted; that people were arrested, they spent up to three months in prison. Then there was another man from Prozor, together with 22 others. The army and the people who were responsible for filing criminal reports did do their work. And a large number of them ended up in detention and were prosecuted. The HVO did what it could. After all, Ivica Rajic was arrested and taken to court. Many were prosecuted. Even Mr. Kordic and Mr. Pasko, they were all prosecuted. Criminal proceedings were instituted, so you cannot say that the HVO did not do anything. I don't know how much you want the HVO to do. More than 200 or 300 people were charged for various crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know what crimes you're talking about or what prosecutions against Mr. Kordic and Mr. Ljubicic you're talking about brought by the HVO. Yes, other -- this Tribunal brought charges, and maybe the State Court in Sarajevo eventually brought charges against Mr. Ljubicic, but I, sir, know of no charge ever brought by any HVO authority against either Mr. Kordic or Mr. Ljubicic. And you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that within the major Operation Pauk or Spider, a large number of people were prosecuted, criminal reports were filed and handed over to the prosecution. That is what the HVO, the Main Staff, and other actors could do, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that the HVO in Herceg-Bosna did not punish, for the most part, crimes against Muslims -- in particular, war crimes against Muslims of the type we're talking about this morning. They either weren't punished because the conduct that -- the underlying conduct that was engaged in was essentially part of the programme, it was part of the Herceg-Bosna project and programme of anti-Muslim policies and actions, mass persecutions, expulsions, imprisonment, deportation and destruction. It was either that or, at bottom, Herceg-Bosna and the HVO didn't really care about crimes committed against Muslims, they just simply didn't count, for the most part; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. Proceedings were instituted for rape, for expulsion, for many other acts, and your witnesses, particularly from Prozor, enumerated the people against whom charges were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at slide number 47 in Sanction which is part of Exhibit P02802. This was a military police report on the 15th of June, 1993. It will be in the, I believe, binder number 3, but we have it in Sanction, both hard copy -- I mean, both the full document and excerpt. But, sir, what this report says, and I submit to you that this summarises the attitude: "Crime/Incident. "No criminal acts or incidents were notified yesterday. Only the ethnical cleansing of the town from persons of Muslim nationality was noticed." No crimes, only the ethnic cleansing of Muslims. That was the pervasive attitude of the HVO, wasn't it? We're just cleaning Muslims; nothing criminal about that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you obviously didn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I object. What the Prosecution has read is his interpretation of what is written there. In the report, it doesn't say anywhere that the author of this report describes as ethnic cleansing that is not considered a crime by the author of this report. That is the Prosecutor's interpretation, and we cannot read documents in this way, nor put questions to the witness on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go to slide number 57, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. General Petkovic, the document that we have just seen, I don't know whether it is the same document, but several months ago, maybe even several years, I already put the question to a witness. I don't remember who now. The document we have in front of us is a document coming from the military police, and this document calls in question at unit -- or accuses an ATG unit which, according to the document, is engaging in ethnic cleansing. I am faced with the following problem, which is quite a simple one. If there is a plan of some scope, everybody's affected, including the military police. And due to this, why is the military police denouncing a unit that is doing this? And I am really asking myself a question. There's something that is not functioning properly. How would you explain that elements of the military police are drawing attention to infractions in relation -- in an official report? And as the Prosecutor says, but that is his opinion, nothing is done because the military police identifies the authors. They are members of the 4th Battalion and Baja Kraljevic ATG units, so all this is clear. Why was nothing done? There is something which is escaping me. Perhaps you can clarify this for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the question that is missing here has been noticed by the military police. It was assigned the task of controlling the town of Mostar on the 1st of June by a decision of the authorities. In this case, there has already been reference to the fact that almost the entire Command of the 4th Battalion, headed by Mladen Misic, was suspended and relieved of duty. We have released the document in this case, and that Mr. Fric [phoen] Coric was appointed instead of him and a new battalion command. Therefore, the command of the operative zone did take certain steps, and the Command of the 4th Battalion, in June, was relieved of duty and a new command was appointed. I do not recall number -- the number of the document, but the document has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me that the commander of the 4th Battalion was suspended. Fine. But the members of the ATG -- Baja Kraljevic ATG, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what happened to the Baja Kraljevic anti-terrorist group. They are Tuta's soldiers. I can't speak of them now. But I can say, regarding the 4th Battalion, that that the command headed by Mladen Misic was relieved of duty in June, expelled from the HVO, and a new team appointed to head the 4th Battalion of the 3rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: This commander of the 1st Company of the 3rd Battalion, Mate Anicic, do you know him or not ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot personally remember. I heard that Mate Anicic does exist as a member of the military police, but I simply can't recall his appearance. He was the commander of a company, so that was a lower level that I did not communicate with. But he does exist as a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Registrar, have you one minute left, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There must be eight -- well, we disagree, Your Honour, with all the interventions this morning. Thank you, I'll take the seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight minutes, eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to table -- slide 57 in Sanction, which is a table titled "HVO Enforcement Actions." Sir, just following up on what you've said, and I put to you that a review of the evidence in the case so far and a review of the available documentation causes me or leads me to put these propositions to you. The HVO clearly had the ability to investigate and prosecute Muslims for alleged "treason and rebellion," and we have evidence of that in the document cited, and it's been discussed in this case. The HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities had the ability to indict Serbs for war crimes. And I will stop there and momentarily go to slide 50, if we can, which is an excerpt of the report which is marked as P04699. In light of what we were saying just these last few moments: "Criminal police working on the prevention of crimes of special state concern (war crimes and terrorism) have filed to the competent military prosecutors a total of 92 criminal charges against 256 persons. The breakdown of these crimes is as follows: four cases of genocide, 31 cases of war crimes against the civilian population, 149 cases of armed rebellion, four cases of crimes committed against prisoners of war, four cases of destruction of important business premises. The persons charged were exclusively of Serbian nationality and all charges were fully documented. In this domain, the criminal police are also continuing work on documenting crimes against the Croatian population by people of Muslim nationality, both military persons and civilians." I put to you, sir, that the numbers -- the cases you were referring to a few moments ago, for the most part, and Judge Trechsel said, and to be very clear, allowing for exceptional cases, I put to you, occasionally against a Croat perpetrator against a Muslim victim, most these cases that you've just mentioned were cases against Serbs and Muslims, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have cited, I don't know whose report it is, of the civilian or the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a report of the HVO HZ-HB, Mr. Prlic's government, for the six-month period from January to June 1993. So it comes from the highest authority. That's the case, wasn't it, sir? I don't have time to debate with you, but that's simply the case. We can see it right here. Serbs and Muslims, those were the people that were being prosecuted, not Croats.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The HVO -- the HVO had the ability -- excuse me, sir, excuse me, sir. [Indiscernible] Mr. Karnavas, apologies, but my time is limited and I do want to try to finish in keeping with the Chamber's time. Item 3, I put it to you that the HVO in Herceg-Bosna could indict Muslims and others for war crimes, not just the Serbs, and we see examples of that below. You could round up -- invest huge efforts in rounding up and prosecuting Croat conscripts not reporting for mobilisation, and HVO soldiers for deserting posts and not obeying orders, including some rather draconian measures. I only have time to mention row 7: "Stojic order directing military courts to give priority to cases involving failure to mobilise," which is 4D01655. Line 11, document P03700, a Praljak order, dated 25th of July, 1993: "Persons disobeying to be disarmed, stripped of their uniforms, detained with no food or water." Line 13, 3D02798, a Bradara order from the Kiseljak area 12 October 1993: "HVO soldiers leaving posts to be shot; commanders of such soldiers to be proclaimed traitors and shot." I mention, as a final example, which the Chamber may recall the evidence in the case, and which you, sir, directed and mounted a major operation to remove people around the Kiseljak area who were threatening Mr. Rajic, and Mr. -- and you remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have chosen the things that suit you, and you didn't wish to take the criminal reports against Croats drafted by certain institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you remember the operation you directed against people that were threatening Mr. Rajic, don't you? You undertook a rather major operation -- a major investment of HVO resources to take what was effective action. You took those people out. They were no longer an issue. I put it to you, sir, that the HVO and Herceg-Bosna, including you, yourself, when you were sufficiently motivated, when you really wanted to, you could take actions, but it wasn't, for the most part, actions against the HVO for crimes against Muslims, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I didn't wish to interrupt my learned friend the Prosecutor until he finished the question relating to document 4699, the number of criminal reports and filed criminal reports, according to this document. But for the transcript, it is important to say that these were reports filed by the civilian police and not the military police, nor is it that part of the report. These are reports filed by the civilian police. And as Mr. Petkovic said, that he didn't know who filed these reports, I think it is worthwhile for us to know who did file them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours? As I don't have did time to go into this, I would just like to show -- Your Honours, if you would look at this, please. This is part of the document shown by Colleague Scott, half of this page, the whole of this page, and up to here on the third page [indicates]. These are all criminal reports for particular criminal acts. Mr. Scott showed you the part relating to war crimes and terrorism. If you look at the beginning of this excerpt on page 24 of the report, you will see that in other chapters there are crimes; murder, rape, and the like. So this is one of the examples how we can mislead the Court by asking questions in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the Prosecutor has only two minutes, but he will be able to use them, but I wish to put my question first so that, within the two minutes, he can come back to it. The Prosecutor tells you that the HVO did nothing regarding prosecution. I remember, on the basis of two documents, and I don't remember the numbers - I didn't know that the Prosecutor would be talking about this - it seems to me you granted an interview regarding the destruction of the Old Bridge, and you explained that the military prosecutor was informed about it. So we have that document. Now, regarding the events in Stupni Do, it seems to me that there is a document which indicates that you also said that the military prosecutor was informed. Do you remember the interview that you gave about the Old Bridge, Stari Most, and the events in Stupni Do, when you said that the military prosecutor had been seized by this, and in the days that immediately follow, not several years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do remember, and it was informed not only for this case but for a host of others which the Prosecutor intentionally skipped over. I think between 200 and 300 criminal reports were filed against members of the HVO who were charged of acts linked to Muslims, and the entire area was cleansed of all criminals who caused problems. And his own witnesses mentioned them by name. They were all arrested, and criminal reports were filed. You remember Mr. Klica, who is still a criminal, and I'm saying this quite openly, though I'm afraid what could happen to my family. They, too -- he, too, was arrested. He spent three months there. Bradic from Prozor, with 20 other men -- or was held in detention for three months in the Heliodrom precisely because of his attitude towards Muslims. The Court did what it did, but I am saying that those who filed criminal reports did so and handed it all over to the judicial authorities, the prosecutor, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I can only respond that if we had more time to go into the particulars, I would debate those points with you vociferously. But the fact of the matter is in terms of the Stupni Do and the issues raised by the President just now, the fact of the matter remains, sir, the HVO, the Herceg-Bosna authorities, did not prosecute, punish, or remove a single HVO officer or soldiers for any crimes concerning the destruction of the Old Bridge or concerning Stupni Do. You can refer reports -- you can refer to reports all day long, sir, but the reality is there were no prosecutions or punishments, and I put it to you at this level, and the reason for all the material I've briefly put before you this morning, Your Honour -- Mr. Petkovic, is because at the structure level it didn't happen. And it wasn't just one or two cases, there were a few, and I've said repeatedly there were a few. But, generally speaking, the HVO structures and authorities did not punish crimes against Muslims. And I put that to you quite clearly, and you know that, don't you? If we could have less --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. For Stupni Do, three or four men, as the main actors, together with the statements, were handed over to the prosecution for further processing. And after all --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No one was prosecuted or punished, and that was my point and that is my question. I move to my final question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what is up to me. I can't go further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petkovic, you know, it's kind of like there's some modern-day weapons, they call them missiles and things, they call them "fire and forget." You fire them off and you forget and they do their own thing. I put it to you, sir, you can't have that attitude at your level. When you're the number one or the number two officer of the HVO, you have armed men out in the field, acting under your orders, under your command, and you can't simply say, Well, I sent a report to someone, and wash your hands of it. You have to take responsibility, you have to take some individual actions, you have to exercise some due diligence to make sure that the army under your control is actually being controlled, that crimes are being prevented, that crimes are being punished, crimes are being disciplined, and you didn't do that in any effective way, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. We did everything we were obliged to do under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. President: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your final question, because have you no more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is my final question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us about when you went to Mr. Boban, and in terms of resigning your number-one position, apparently because -- something about Operation Jug and the fact that someone else -- your advice had been, in your view, disregarded, I simply put to you now, sir, and it is my final question: Did you ever consider resigning either because of the crimes that the HVO was carrying out on a systematic basis, under your direction, or because of your inability to prevent and punish the massive crimes being committed against the Muslims? Did you ever consider or offer to resign over that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are your constructions which I reject. I resigned because of everything that was happening, and that included some of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination. I appreciate the Court's indulgence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. You finished within the 20 minutes you had available. I think the Stojic Defence has 30 minutes now, and then Ms. Alaburic will conclude. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could the usher please come and collect some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, you'll be given the documents now, but I will start right now. Yes, those are your documents. Yesterday, Mr. Petkovic, on the 9th of March, 2010, on page 64 of the transcript, lines 20 to 21 -- please listen to me, because I don't have much time, and I'll show all the documents so there won't be any problems. So on page 64, line 20 to 21, in response to a question put by the Prosecution about who was to care about individuals who were detained and isolated pursuant to your order of the 30th of June, 1993, number 3019, P3019, you said that there was a decree according to which the Defence Department was to be -- respond to both of the centres where these individuals were taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, there is such a decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please have a look at P292, the first document in the binder. Mr. Petkovic, is that the decree that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't have to go any further. It's an exhibit. We'll be brief. Have a look at the following document, P452. They are all in order, in the order we are following. It's a decision on establishing a central military prison in the territory of the HZ-HB as part of the Heliodrom Barracks. Mr. Petkovic, have you seen a different document that shows that the head of the Defence Department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, established any other prison, apart from this Central Military Prison, in accordance with the decree that we've just had a look at?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know who established --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, please be brief. I'm asking you whether you saw any such document.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that several military investigative prisons were established in 1992, where POWs and detainees were to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This just has to do with the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, please answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I had seen --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. I asked you whether you had seen a decision of any other kind in which Mr. Stojic established a centre or a prison in accordance with the decree that we have already seen, and I'm excluding the one that we have before us. We'll deal with military prisons. I'm not avoiding the subject. We'll see who was responsible for them. But I'm asking you whether, with regard to these centres for POWs, you saw any other documents, apart from the one that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision on establishing a central military prison, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. We'll move on. Mr. Petkovic, with regard to the units that disarmed and isolated its own members of Muslim nationality pursuant to your order of the 30th of June, 1993, were these units responsible for filing criminal reports against them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, criminal reports had to be filed when there was a division made in centres where they were gathered, but not at that point in time, and SIS organs and the Crimes Services worked in that field.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I'm asking you whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I'm awfully sorry, but I find it difficult to understand your last questions, lines 15 and following. Perhaps there is a problem with the translation: "With regard to the units that disarmed and isolated its own members of Muslim nationality pursuant to your order of 30 June, were these units responsible for filing criminal reports against them?" Again whom? Against the disarmed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petkovic understood it in that way, and he answered my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, my question was whether the units that isolated them had the responsibility of filing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal reports had to be filed by SIS employees and by crime police employees, so that is, I suppose, part of their work when bringing them in and processing each individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, this is the third time I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the commanders of units. Were they responsible for filing such reports?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Crime Service and the SIS Service had to process each case and file a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that a, Yes, or a, No?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, no, not the commander, but the services whose work it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at P4745. It's the following document, Mr. Petkovic. It's an exhibit, and this is your order to the operations zone and to the immediately-subordinated units. You ordered them -- the date is the 2nd of September. You said that all units in this operative zone should be cleansed of members of Muslim nationality, they should be disarmed and isolated, and criminal procedures should be instigated against those who had committed crimes, and other legal measures should be taken. Mr. Petkovic, is this your order? You provided it to the operative zone and immediately-subordinated units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they will use the organs that are responsible for criminal processing. That is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, a minute ago you said that that wasn't the responsibility of units. This document --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question, Your Honours, because the previous question concerned the issue of whether one should file a criminal report against disarmed and isolated members of the Muslim nationality; whereas this document has to do with crime reports that are filed against perpetrators of crimes, so it doesn't concern all Muslim HVO soldiers who have been isolated. So we're dealing with two completely different issues here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, perhaps you can be of assistance to us with regard to the Muslims who were disarmed. You're not a jurist, but if you're a general, you have a fairly extensive scope of competence. If you have an army under your command, you know that -- well, I don't have the relevant legal provisions, but there are two violations; there's treason and there is mutiny. There is desertion, there is desertion. You can say "mutiny" or "treason." In an army, if you suspect that there might be a mutiny or treason on behalf of your own soldiers, or they might try to take control of the army, could there be cases of prosecution in the Penal Code of the JNA that you're familiar with? Perhaps you can find the answer, but in the Herceg-Bosna code were there provisions for this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are provisions, Your Honours. This is the 2nd of September, 1993, when the 1st and 3rd Brigade there were perhaps 30 to 40 members of Muslim nationality who had remained there, and this was a time when the people laid an ambush and about - I'm not sure of the exact number - 12 to 13 members of the HVO, who were Croats, were killed. The Muslims who remained in the HVO carried out a task in September, but they carried out a massacre on 10 to 12 Croats, and then they fled to Blagaj. So these are people who remained in the HVO and who, through their acts, committed a crime. This does not concern those who had been disarmed and brought into detention centres. We all know what happened in the Gubavica area. It's a group of Muslims that we detained. They had remained in the HVO. They were supposed to be loyal, but they committed a serious crime. They killed a number of HVO members, and this is what the issue is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to the September case, it's clear. But as for those whom you disarmed on the 30th of June and on the following days, did you disarm them because they were going to commit an act of mutiny or because they were going to betray you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were disarmed for preventive reasons, for general security reasons, because up until the Gubavica area the ABiH, with HVO Muslim members, had taken control, and their objective was to go further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, let's move on to another document that has to do with filing criminal reports, and that will partially answer the question put by Judge Antonetti. The document is P5581. Have you found it? In this document, Mr. Siljeg forwards your order that we have seen to immediately-subordinated units. Mr. Petkovic, the individuals here -- well, in fact, it has to do with cleansing units of members of Muslim nationality. To be precise, you said that criminal reports should be filed for those who had committed crimes. You said that criminal proceedings should be instigated, and other legal measures should be taken, others should be detained and isolated. So here there were individuals for whom you believed that they had committed crimes, and in some cases you had no reason to believe they had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please don't answer in general terms. I'm asking you the following: You can see that two categories are at stake here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If anyone was known to have committed a crime, that person would be prosecuted immediately. Everyone else is being processed, interviewed, heard. The SIS organs and the Crime Service carries out the relevant procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are these the organs and the units of Mr. Siljeg as it says here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to have a look at the order dated the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and the witness please slow down and pause between question and answer, as the interpreter cannot follow at this speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we'll see the documents dated the 10th of August as well. My question is quite specific: When you said that the SIS organs and the other organs processed the others, these orders in these units to whom Mr. Siljeg forwarded this order. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these are organs and units or whether they are SIS centres in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know, so we will move on. Mr. Petkovic, did unit commanders compile records about those who had been arrested and imprisoned? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had records that were kept in the units so that they could know whom their soldiers were. They didn't go to detention units to compile lists there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please have a look at 2120. It's an order from Mr. Lasic that confirms what you have just said; isn't that correct? He says it's being forwarded to all subordinated units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Ms. Nozica. I think that there is a problem with regard to the reference. I just wanted to check something in the document. P5581, the order from Colonel Siljeg, refers to the order from the Main Staff dated the 2nd of October, 1993. I also checked the B/C/S version. The reference was -- or, rather, the date is the same, the 2nd of October, 1993. But when we have a look at General Petkovic's order, it seems to me that the date is the 2nd of September, 1993; document P4745. Have you noticed this? Is it the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, yes, it's the same document. They are both Prosecution documents, but you are correct. In the original text, the date is wrong. That's in document P5581. But you can see, by the numbers, that in P5581 a reference is made to P4745. That's when you have a look at the numbers under which these documents have been delivered. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we were looking at P2120, and we said that that was precisely what you were saying whereby the units keep the records. It was Lasic's order.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was up to the units to state how many people were detained or not, but they don't go to the detention centres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I mean, we really lose time when we, every five minutes, have to recall this. This is a matter -- I mean, I understand your temperament, and it's a good thing, but it is really not only not helpful, but it is a pity. Put your foot on the brake.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do understand you, but my time is really very short and I have to, in a way, stop and interrupt the witness if I don't need a further explanation, and that's when this overlapping occurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petkovic, did you issue orders on moving -- relocating the district civilian prison in Mostar to the area of the investigative prison at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the request of the Ministry of the Interior and the Justice Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at this order, which is document P2925. Have you found it, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what it's about. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From this document, we can see that the Defence Department was not informed about it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. They were asking for the relocation --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, take a look at document P4188, please. This is your order, and we've already seen it during the examination-in-chief. Tell me now, you say here -- well, you explained why you asked for the prisoners to be made presentable, but I'm interested in something else. Does it follow from this document that you knew that the prisoners, the ones that we -- that you referred to in the document, came under the authority of Mr. Siljeg, and that's why you were addressing him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the nine prisons were under the authority of the Defence Department, so we can stop any discussions of that kind and Mr. Siljeg. This was one of the nine prisons that came under the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I'm going to tell you under whose authority they came under in due course. Just be patient. Let's look at the next document, which is P1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. General Petkovic, when there is a document, sometimes one can read it in two ways, incriminating and exculpatory. In the document I discovered, under 2 and 1, one learns that there is the European Community that is inquiring into the problem. And then you speak of Prozor, and you say, Show them the detainees, but make them presentable. Why do you say that? Normally, a detainee should always be presentable. Why are you saying, Make them presentable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's always meant that somebody should go into the room, the premises, to see if everything is in order or if there is disorder in a room. So you can only ask somebody to button up his shirt if it's unbuttoned, or things like that, nothing more than that. And it's the custom that when somebody is coming to visit, that you see that the situation is put in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this sentence should be interpreted as a simple instruction so that the area of the penitentiary should be in order, and it doesn't apply to the physical appearance of the detainees; is that -- is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, precisely. Well, you can't put a prisoner in order. All you can do is, if they're untidy and if their shirt is unbuttoned, to ask them to button their shirts up, if somebody's going to talk to them, and put their room in order. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Take a look at the next document, which is P1959, please. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, this one of your orders, and it's an exhibit, dated the 18th of April. And in point 2, you say that: "The exchange of prisoners, both soldiers and civilians, shall start immediately." And you're sending this order to the operative zones, and you are asking them to inform all the HVO units of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Petkovic. We're going to move on. That's fine, you've answered. Now let's look at document P5138, which is the same type of order, except this one is dated the 17th of September, 1993. And in point 3, you say: "Secure the release of all prisoners by the 21st of September, 1993." And you're once again sending that out to all the operative zones. And in item 5, you are asking the commanders to forward this order urgently to subordinate units; is that right, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The declaration of Tudjman and Izetbegovic was common knowledge to everybody, and I'm just translating that down to the level of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I take it that your answer is, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing to the units, whereas the declaration was --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, the documents speak for themselves, they're quite clear. All I want you to confirm is that whether this is a document of yours.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, and we'll see who was in charge of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. General Petkovic, we saw this morning a series of documents signed by you in various areas. I note, like this one, that these documents are signed, though the Chief of Staff is General Praljak, and I see you signing documents which could come under the competence of General Praljak; specifically, the consequences of a Tudjman-Izetbegovic declaration. And I ask myself, proceeding from that, whether the change of function in the month of July, did it really take place. Did you, in fact, become number two, because these are important documents that you are signing and which could come under the competence of number one, and number one is General Praljak? How, then, did it happen that this document was not signed by General Praljak? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, in this trial we saw General Praljak's permission giving me permission to sign this document. And it says that I'm signing pursuant to the authorisation of the commander, with the authorisation of the commander. So I asked General Praljak whether I could talk to Delic and discuss the military part of the Tudjman-Izetbegovic declaration, especially with respect to items 1 and 3. And it says at the bottom there: "With the authorisation of the commander." And so I was given authorisation by General Praljak to attend negotiations and to be able to sign the document, which is what I did. So this was the Tudjman-Izetbegovic declaration. After the declaration, the Dretelj Prison was disbanded. And it was my duty to inform my commanders what had been going on, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I take note of what you're saying. But you say that this led to the closing of the Dretelj Prison; fine. I remember that General Praljak, when he was in your place, told us that the prisons were not his competence. Could that explain that he didn't wish to sign this type of document and he passed on this competence to you? I don't know. It's a hypothesis on my part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when General Praljak arrived, then UNPROFOR was informed that I would be conducting negotiations further with the three other parties on behalf of the Croatian Defence Council and that General Praljak would not be attending the negotiations. So he authorised me, and, for that reason, I continued to conduct the negotiations. And every time I would sign in his name, with his authorisation. This was the Tudjman-Izetbegovic declaration mentioning the release of prisoners of war, and, in item 3, it referred to mixed committee meetings who would be working on the subject of releasing the prisoners. And it was my duty to inform my commanders what would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we're now going to move on and discuss the prisons, the centres for isolation in all the operative zones, to see who was in charge of them, as you said a moment ago. And for that, let's look at P1478, which is a piece of information conveying the order issued by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic and the Command of the Central Bosnia Operations Zone on the 12th of February, where it says that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic had issued an order that the military prison comes under the authority of the command of the operations zone. Now, Mr. Petkovic, is that what it says in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the authority was, but that's what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's move on now to the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone. And for that, let's look at P3234, the next document. This is an order from Mr. Siljeg, dated the 6th of July. It's already an exhibit, and we've looked at it a number of times in this courtroom, about the detention of all Muslim men aged between 16 to 60. Now, Mr. Petkovic, did you know that Mr. Siljeg had issued an order of this kind and detained all Muslim men, as he says here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this order, we can see that he didn't inform anybody about it, but probably he did implement it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see, probably did implement it. Right. Let's move on to the next document, which is 2D268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question was: "Did you know that Mr. Siljeg had passed this order?" And the answer was: "We can see he didn't inform anybody about it, but probably he did implement it." That is not an answer to the question, Mr. Petkovic. The question was, Did you know? I would like to hear the answer, even if counsel does not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 6th of July, I did not know Siljeg had issued such an order, because he didn't send it to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He kept it to himself or for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about on the 14th of August, Mr. Petkovic? Did you know about it when you sent the letter which is P4188, the meeting of the heads of the European Community where you spoke about the prisoners that should be brought in? Did you know that Mr. Siljeg had detained them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said if there were any. If there were any detainees, was my wording, I believe, so take a look at the document, show them if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, you didn't write that. You said, If there was something in Prozor. And then in brackets it says "detainees."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if there were detainees, show them, but I didn't know whether there were any. And I was saying that if there were, that they should be shown them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, this is precisely the reason why I couldn't follow on from the question that Mr. Trechsel asked. When did you learn that Mr. Siljeg actually detained people and that he had people detained who were Muslim men? When did you learn about that, that that had been done?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you -- well, I can't give you the date, because at that point in time, I did not know whether there were or were not any Muslim detainees in Prozor. Now, the European Community asked about this, and I asked to go and see, and I said that if there were any, he had to show them to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, did you know about this in 1993? What I'm asking you is whether, from that point in time to the end of 1993, did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go to Prozor during that time. I was handing over my duty at that time, so I didn't have to know about all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, let's take a look at who was in charge of the prisons in this area. And for that, let's look at 2D268, the next document, which is already an exhibit, Mr. Petkovic. And here the unit commander, the commander of the Rama Brigade, is appointing a prison warden, Mr. Petar Baketaric [phoen], and he is putting him in charge of the detainees' security, accommodation, and so on. Now let's look at the next document relating to that same topic, which is P4156, and here we have the same commander. The same day, an order is being issued about prisoners of war and persons temporarily detained, and he's saying where the prisoners of war should be put up and where the others should be put up. He speaks about security, food, and accommodation; is that right, is that what we can deduce from these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this prison comes under the Defence Department. Now, why would I know about this on the 13th of August? I wasn't in Prozor and I wasn't in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you are here under oath. The document shows that the commander of the unit had appointed a warden. Now, whether he came under the Defence Department or not is speculation on your part, so we can now move on, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not speculation, madam, and I ask you to put the document on the table so that we can see whose authority the prisons came under.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, let's see what was actually going on, just briefly, Mr. Petkovic; short answers, please. Look at P3151, the next document, please, which is an order from Mr. Nedjeljko Obradovic, dated the 3rd of July. And in this order, he, referring to the Main Staff order, says under point 4, what should be done with members of the Muslims in the units. And he says that those whom you do not leave in the units should be disarmed and incarcerated. Did you know this order by Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I and Mr. Stojic wrote the order on reorganisation. We wrote it together, so of course I know about this order by Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down. We're not able to translate at this pace and overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, P3161. Mr. Obradovic, by this order dated the 3rd of July, is saying that there shall be no visits in Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski prisons. He is forbidding visits, and this is a way of commanding and being in charge of the prisons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the last day when Mr. Obradovic was supposed to hand over these prisons to somebody else, under somebody else's authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, let's look at P3197 now, please. This is an order whereby Mr. Obradovic is forming a medical commission for Gabela, Dretelj, and Heliodrom prisons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is the 5th of July, the date you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, and relax because it's not your time that will be going. Mr. Petkovic, shortly ago you said, and that was a document dated 3rd of July: "This was the last day when Mr. Obradovic was supposed to hand over these prisons." And now we have a document dated the 5th of July, two days later, and apparently he has not handed over the prison. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can, indeed. We've seen the document of the Military Police Company in Dretelj that is requesting for medical aid and is addressing the surgery in Capljina, and it is normal for the -- Obradovic to intervene. And upon their request, he sent a medical team there. So the documents are being shown that people do not wish to connect to previous documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Petkovic. I probably was not able to express myself properly. With regard to a document dated 3rd of July, this said -- you said this was the last day that Mr. Obradovic -- I'm interpreting what you said, but it's difficult to read it otherwise -- that Mr. Obradovic was responsible for this prison, because the next day or the same day he was giving it away. So it is not normal if, two days later, when, according to what you have said before, he was not in charge of the prison anymore, he issues an order concerning this prison. And I -- maybe you were in error when you said that it was the last day that Mr. Obradovic had not yet handed over the prison or something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not in error. On the 3rd of July, the order was written that the 1st Brigade had nothing to do with the prisons. And on the 5th, upon the request of a military police company that addressed a request to the Medical Office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Stop. We won't waste time. You're not answering the question. Please continue, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your Honour -- His Honour Judge Trechsel is talking about document 3201.
