utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I co-operated most and had the best co-operation with Mrs. Antunovic, because I was her immediate subordinate or she was my immediate superior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At this meeting of the 13th of April, 1999 -- and, Your Honours, I have provided a separate document, 4D2040, for you, if you wish to take a look at it. Mr. Markica Rebic, among other things, said of you, General, the following, and you can listen to me: "Apart from that, his position was very interesting. He was not a man who could be linked to a few key matters, so he would have been charged long ago." I don't want to burden you with the details. There are numerous details, excerpts, variations on a topic, and so on and so forth. Now, my question to you, General, is this: May we have your comments to what Mr. Markica Rebic says, that you weren't somebody who could be connected to any key events that took place in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I suppose Markica Rebic followed the events, and he drew that conclusion on the basis of the information he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, any of the people attending this meeting, or anybody else, for that matter, did they call you before your testimony in the Blaskic trial and express their concern about what you were going to testify about and whether you would defend Croatia in a suitable manner at the trial?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody contacted me or spoke to me in that sense, either before or after the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, Mr. Scott, among other things, showed you your curriculum vitae in which -- and it is document P8731, in which you stated that you had been a member of the HDZ from 1992. And you said that this CV was compiled in 1996 and that sometime in 1998 or 1999, you were stricken from the HDZ list. Now, my question to you is: Which HDZ are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ of the Republic of Croatia. They struck me from their list, but they didn't tell me the exact date when I was stricken from party membership and when I was registered in the first place, which is something I asked them to do and provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the Stojic Defence, General, asked you a question. They asked you whether Bruno Stojic could issue operative orders to HVO units. And that was on page 50089 of the transcript and the next page. And your answer to that was that he could have done that on the basis of Article 30 of the Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB. And after that, Defence counsel said, Yes, you're quite right, that possibility did exist. And let's look at document P588 briefly, P588, which is the Decree on the Armed Forces. Let's look at Article 30 of that decree. And in para 2 of Article 30, it says the supreme commander of the armed forces can transfer the performance of certain duties of control and command of the armed forces to the head of the Defence Department. And then within the frameworks of his remit, the head of the Defence Department shall enact regulations, decisions, and other acts and documents. And the last paragraph, it says: "For his work, the head of the Defence Department shall be responsible to the supreme commander for the affairs given to him within his remit." Tell us, please, General, in mentioning Article 30, are those the provisions that you had in mind, the ones I quoted?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the ones. They're all contained in Article 30. There are no others.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you interpret that last paragraph, which says that the head of the Defence Department, with respect to these issues, shall be responsible to the commander. What does that mean vis-a-vis the position of the head of the Defence Department towards the HVO HZ-HB or, rather, the government?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the government is concerned, that is not important. The person to whom this authority is conveyed shall be responsible to the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- I don't think you've answered my question. What I want to ask you is this: The affairs concerning supreme command, now, does the head of the Defence Department have anything to do with the government or is he linked exclusively to the supreme commander for those matters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those cases, he would only be linked to the supreme commander. The government has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since we're looking at this document, Mr. Scott pointed out Article 86 of this decree, relating to the official oath, and it is in 50490, the answer. General, did you ever count how many times the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina is mentioned in this provision, in this article?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did count. I think there are over 20 articles in which Bosnia-Herzegovina is mentioned in the first place in P588, that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, did you take part in preparing this article?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have anything at all to do with the wording of this official oath?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, give us your personal opinion here. Would it have been better if, in that oath, mention was made of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it is mentioned in the other 20 times in these articles?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been better, but I don't think that that is to the detriment of any person of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We saw the Mujahedin's oath and Alija Izetbegovic's. Now, is that a state oath or not is debatable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, look at the next document, please, with respect to the transference of authority. 4D1276 is the document I'd like us to look at next, 4D1276. Yes, that's right. And this the Croatian Law on Defence, and I'd like us to look at Article 47 together, third para from the bottom, in which it is stated that the supreme commander of the armed forces can transfer certain affairs of command and control of the armed forces to the minister, except matters relating to the armed forces -- the use of the armed forces. Now, in your understanding of this article, could Franjo Tudjman transferred to Gojko Susak the authorisations under the Decree on the Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a better read of that, more careful read of that, General. Read it again. You have it on your screen, so read it carefully, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom in to that, because I have trouble seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Listen, General. May we see the right-hand side of the Croatian page, the right-hand column, please, in Croatian. The upper part of the page, the right-hand corner of the page. Right. And it says: "The supreme commander can transfer to the minister of defence certain affairs of control and command over the armed forces, except affairs on the tasks related to the deployment and use of the armed forces." That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Franjo Tudjman, could he transfer the deployment and use of the armed forces to Gojko Susak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, obviously not. That is the exception.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if you know this provision on Herceg-Bosna, which is P588, that restriction or limitation, was it applicable to transference of authority in Herceg-Bosna? And we can go back to the document if you wish to have another look at it. It is P588, Article 30. Does that limitation exist or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Herceg-Bosna, it says -- well, this article does not exist, as it does in the original here. It does not exist and apply to Herceg-Bosna. The Decree on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna, that does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, the Stojic Defence asked you a number of questions, among them whether Bruno Stojic ever issued an operative order of any kind to you. And your answer was that he had not done so, and that the two of you co-signed certain orders, but that he didn't issue any operative orders to you. I'm now going to show you a few documents, and I'm going to ask you to clarify what is meant by "operative" or "operational orders." The first of those documents is P610. This is a daily report of the Military Police Administration, dated the 21st of October, 1992, and it says: "Because of the events in Central Bosnia, upon orders from the head of the Defence Department, we have sent reinforcement from the 2nd Battalion." And it goes on to say that they will continue working in accordance with the Command of Central Bosnia and with the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police. Tell me, General, this sending of a unit as a reinforcement, is it an operative order or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, but it's not addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document P619. It is a report of the Military Police Administration, dated the 22nd of October, 1992. And in the second paragraph, it says: "In view of the conflict in Central Bosnia, in the morning hours the situation in Mostar has deteriorated. Upon orders from the head of the Defence Department and based on the decision of the Presidency of the HVO, during the day we have captured the following features in town: The post office building, the MUP centre, the police station, and we have stopped the work of Radio Mostar BH. In addition, we have also blocked all the roads and took all the check-points in town." I leave out a part of the document, and then I continue with the report that: Participating in the operation were about 500 military police, two anti-terrorist groups commanded by Andabak, members of the Bruno Busic Regiment, members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion, members of the Ljubuski Training Centre, members of the Department of the Interior, and some units of the Mostar Brigade. Tell us, General, can such an order be considered an operative order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not addressed directly to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can make an objection. I consider this improper examination in the redirect. On page 102, in the first line, the question put to Mr. Petkovic was whether Mr. Stojic had issued him any operative orders. Then she went on to discuss a number of documents, that is, two documents, and the witness answered in both cases that these were not operative orders issued to him by Mr. Stojic. I think that my learned friend, at this point, is doing the Prosecution's work. She is incriminating Mr. Stojic without any basis in the questions and answers in the cross-examination. I wish this to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't know where you're going. I understood, like everyone else, that the minister of defence did not have the possibility of giving operative orders. That is not so in Croatia. Article 30, concerning Herceg-Bosna, this is not evident. But if we look closely at Article 30, we can draw the conclusion that the defence minister can delegate competencies of a purely administrative nature and not of an operative nature. But what exactly do you wish to show, having said that, because the objection of Mr. Nozica is well founded. What do you wish to show? Put your question. You're wasting a great deal of time, through a large number of documents, whereas the simplest procedure would be to ask a question and then show him a document, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is what I'm doing now. But I wish to draw attention to a part of your statement, that you and everyone else in this courtroom know that the defence minister did or did not do things, that is, he did not have the ability to issue operative orders. If I may remind you, three years ago, in this courtroom, there were allegations, that it is well known, that the defence minister in America or wherever has nothing to do with the army and that, therefore, why we are discussing the position and role of a defence minister in trials of this kind relating to war crimes. What you're saying today shows that in the past three and a half years, you haven't changed your opinion, and that in spite of everything that we have tried to do in this courtroom, with the aim of clarifying events, has not reached you to this day. I take note of this, and in view of this, I will organise myself for the continuation of these proceedings. But what we wish to tell you is the following: that General Petkovic has never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're saying that, You haven't changed your opinion, but I have no opinion, I have no position. Why are you saying that, You have not changed your position? We don't have a position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me quote you. Page 103, lines 23 to 25: [In English] "I understood, like everyone else, that the minister of defence did not have the possibility of giving operative orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Let me finish. Similar observations as to what a defence minister has as his competencies or not have been made during this trial, and, if necessary, I can find those places from the transcript going back three years, all the statements saying that it is well known that the defence minister has a role or doesn't have one. I fully understand a common-sense position that crimes were committed by soldiers and that military commanders are, therefore, responsible. Fully understanding such a common-sense position that I, too, would probably have if I was dealing with a case in Rwanda or some other country, in these proceedings we have tried to specify for you who is competent for what, de jure, and also the situation de facto. We have endeavoured, in making our case, to rely always on regulations and documents. We have never shown you a document that was not based on rules. And the situation, with 10.000 documents in this case, is as follows: You can find a document in support of any thesis you may have. What you have to do, as Judges, is to find your way in this forest of documents to find what is the rule and what is the exception, what is de jure and what is de facto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I have been listening to you. Does that mean - I'm trying to understand your theory - is that the defence minister does have the possibility of issuing operational orders? Is that what you're trying to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I've already demonstrated that on the basis of the reports which Mr. Valentin Coric, as head of the military police demonstration, filed in December 1992, it is quite clear that this is an order of an operational nature. What I wish to tell you is the following: that when we're speaking of certain situations, that we have to make a distinction from one situation to the next, because some combat orders may have been issued by General Petkovic, some combat orders may have been issued by someone in the chain of command subordinate to Mr. Petkovic, but there are also situations when that is not so. And in my opinion, you simply have to be informed about these things so as to assess each situation individually, taking into account all the evidence, rather than having a single, unified position, all crimes were committed by soldiers and the commanders are responsible. You have to bear in mind the various competencies of various bodies, and for this purpose one needs a very detailed analysis. We are aware that we have entered this courtroom with a position of minus 10, that it is quite commonsensical to consider that military commanders are responsible because some of their soldiers committed the crimes, and we realise that our attempt to present our case in this courtroom will be very difficult, that very often you will think that we are thinking the responsibility to someone else, rather than trying to clearly explaining the relationships. We were aware that all the colleagues in the so-called civilian authorities would be against us, we were aware of all this, and from the first day we wanted to have a principled position in this courtroom. And if someone shows me that any thesis of General Petkovic's Defence is contrary to the rules and what was happening on the ground as a rule, we will not say a further word in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm most grateful. My learned friend's response is perhaps revealing. I'm not going to seek to dissect it, but I will make a couple of observations, with the Court's leave. It is, of course, not the role of a Bench to be inordinately patient, to be inordinately lenient with any party, whether it be the Defence or the Prosecution. It is for the Bench to navigate its way through the evidence, consistent with the Rules, in a manner that enables them to come to a fair determination of the matter that is being adjudicated. Now, at times, of course, my learned friend's intervention may have had the flavour of an apology somewhat as a victim, but the propositions that any party comes into this court with a minus 10 is a victim psychology which, in my respectful submission, has no basis before professional judges. It may appease the conscience of individuals, for counsel in a case, but the reality is, and the objective evidence, in my respectful submission, shows that the Bench are alive to their responsibilities. Now, on many occasions, Mr. President, you and your colleagues have said, with many witnesses and in relation to many objections, that you have not come to any conclusion in relation to this matter. You have said it repeatedly, I think only a couple of weeks ago, that will be done once the hearing is finished, and you'll adjudicate and consider all the evidence in the round. But simply to repeatedly or assert that a view has been taken or a view has not changed is simply a recipe for disaster and is, indeed, a complete -- completely self-indulgent. Your Honours, apart from the homilies that were contained in the intervention, the crux of the matter, in my respectful submission, may go down to something that my learned friend Mr. Karnavas says: That lawyers, of course, may have a variety of theories. What is important is the evidence you hear from the witness. The views of counsel will be marshaled from the Prosecution and from the Defence at an appropriate juncture. That juncture is not today, in this courtroom, at half past one. It will be in closing briefs and in closing speeches. But, Your Honours, a question was put in cross-examination to the witness, who is under oath. That was unequivocal in its scope. It is whether or not my client -- our client issued him operative orders. Now, my learned friend can seek to -- I won't say blur the issues, but may ask any question she wishes, provided its relevant and its probative. Your Honour asked a very straightforward question regarding the purpose of this questioning and its relevance. Your Honours, in that ream of response, in that long speech that was given by my learned friend for General Petkovic, of course, in his presence, a response is perhaps difficult to discern. Your Honours, I would enjoy, and all of us, myself included, to be rather disciplined in our interventions so as not to waste the Court's time and to make sure that we do what we are required, which is to enable Your Honours to have the relevant information to make a proper decision. Your Honours, that's all I have to say on this matter, unless my learned friend Ms. Nozica has anything additional to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question, Mr. Khan. I'm not a cook at all. I'm always interested in recipes. And you have spoken for a recipe for disaster, which I did not quite understand. And fearing that I might contribute to disaster, I'm anxious to know, as precisely as possible, what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise if I wasn't clear. And I'm a terrible cook. A cheese sandwich and an omelette, perhaps, is as much as I can make. But, Your Honour, what I was trying to say is when a party engages on a line of questioning which may not be focused and which may not be relevant, a number of consequences occur. Not only is court time wasted, but collateral issues are raised which either require additional time or raise the temperature in the courtroom. And, of course, getting to the truth in an unnecessarily heated environment is not conducive to the ascertainment of the truth, and that is one of the reasons why we have rules, so that the evidence can be sifted and analysed and reviewed, if not in a sterile environment, at least, as far as counsel is concerned, in as dispassionate or, at the very least, in as objective a manner as is possible. And that's what I was saying about a recipe for disaster, if individuals simply say whatever they want regardless of legal discipline and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to join Colleague Khan, and I would add something. I shall try not to be blunt in what I am saying, but I think that each one of us following these proceedings does not understand what exactly we are listening to. Is this an examination-in-chief, a cross-examination of one's own witness, or a closing statement, closing brief? Ms. Alaburic has asked Mr. Petkovic a direct question, whether he had received an operative order from Mr. Stojic. He answers, No. After that, she shows him documents which she thinks show the opposite; in other words, she is provoking an answer from him and is cross-examining him. After all this, all of us in the courtroom are delivered a speech, which is like a closing statement, an analysis of the proceedings. And I'd just like to join Mr. Khan in saying that we have to be careful in conducting our own examination. We are creating unnecessary nervousness in the courtroom, and I don't think it is leading anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am interested in is the document, and a document is important, and I have a question to put to General Petkovic which I believe will summarise everything. General Petkovic, you have listened to all these interventions, and you have understood what they wanted to say. We have a document, P619, coming from Mr. Coric, related to an operation conducted on the 22nd of October, 1992, linked to the situation in Mostar. And we learn that buildings have been taken control of; the post office, MUP, Radio Mostar, et cetera. I won't go into the details. For you, this document, what is it? Is it a document of a military operation, a document regarding security by the police? Does it come under orders that may be issued by the head of the Defence Department to officials in the military police? How would you interpret this document, beyond going into the competencies of one or other involved, one or other party involved? What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document says that according to an order from the head of the Defence Department, the following was done. So this is a report from the military police about the tasks that they received and carried out. It's not just the military police. The military police also mentioned some HVO units that were also assigned such tasks. So obviously there was an order that the military police acted on, as well as some of the HVO units, and the military police forwarded a report as ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this event of the 22nd of October, do you remember it? Was it a joint operation between military units and military police units? Do you remember this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember some of these facilities were placed under the control of HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I just wish to state that I find merits in the objections of both Mr. Khan and Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, and find it also difficult to see what this document has to do with the Defence of Mr. Petkovic, because it seems to concern two other accused, mainly; namely, Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric. And I -- perhaps you can explain, Ms. Alaburic, why you think that this is relevant to the Defence of Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, gladly. I hope you have some understanding for General Petkovic's position too. One of the issues that's important in this courtroom is the issue as to whether orders to go into combat for any military unit of the HZ-HB were orders exclusively by military commanders or whether they were also issued by others. The Petkovic Defence is interested in demonstrating how certain combat operations were carried out following orders issued by someone else and not by a military commander, and we've treated the document in this way. We've tried to show that a certain combat operation was carried out on the basis of an order issued by a president of a certain municipality. What we want to show Your Honours is that we cannot just assume that some military commander organised an action and that that action was carried out because it was ordered by a military commander, because perhaps that wasn't the case. So we are just trying to say that each situation has to be looked into on an individual basis. When you examine the conflict in Gornji Vakuf or in any other location - I just took Gornji Vakuf as an example - when you do that, it will be important to determine whose order was being followed when action was taken. So we just want to define certain matters and this presumption is rebuttable. We want to show you documents to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I might just react in one sentence. I think that makes perfect sense if you are dealing with some fact imputed to Mr. Petkovic. This is -- I fail to see this link here, and that's why I think I was correct and you are not. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas -- Mr. Karnavas, one second. I'll let you have a second, but in 25 minutes I will be here again for a day that will be even worse than this morning, so please hurry up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, a part of -- the technique that's being used is to sabotage the rest of us by bringing these sort of topics at this stage of the proceedings. That's part of the problem. It's for direct examination. But also when counsel says that somehow everybody is against her and she hasn't done anything contrary to the Rules, perhaps you may feast on this for the rest of the day, when the general says that when a soldier commits a crime after he leaves, while he's still a soldier, he's still mobilised, and that the military is not responsible for that, I think if we look at P00425, which is the Code of Military Discipline, and when considering that the general, himself, albeit he did get his grades rather quickly after being a lieutenant-colonel, was a professor, himself, at a military academy, it shocks the conscience for someone to say they're not under the military. This is a clear shifting of the burden, which they're entitled to do. But when they do this at this stage of the game, then it does cause us some concern, because the question is: Are we entitled to ask for re-cross-examination? I'm not suggesting that I will, but I am suggesting that if we're going to allow these sorts of tactics, there are some reactions to that and there are some consequences to be paid. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wish everyone a good day. You will be fortunate enough to have a rest this afternoon, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
